chapter: Los Angeles bands and theater pits, 1927-30
title: Burlesque shows, the hard book and an all-white revue
summary: He explains the Follies and Burbank burlesque shows, the demanding music of all types, and that the show and bands were segregated.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Tell us a little bit about the Follies, on Main Street. Wasn't it on Main Street?
That's right, they both were on Main Street. The Follies was up at Fourth and Main and the Burbank was at Sixth and Main.
Tell us a little bit about the shows; what they were like.

Well, they were burlesque shows, you know, they had strippers and I can remember when Reb Spikes opened up the Follies, I was supposed to go with him. After Reb Spikes left, George Brown took it over around '28, and then
Dalton wanted to open up another burlesque because it was going so good up there, and that was the Burbank Theater at Sixth and Main. That's when I started with them, January, 1929.
That was, I consider, the hardest job I ever had and most responsible job I've ever had.
Were you playing continuously for the dances?
There were regulars; the show would be about an hour and then we'd have a break before the picture was going on. Three shows a day and four on Saturdays.
What do you think made it so difficult for you? Why was it such a hard job?
The music we had to play, it was all types of music, ballet music, overtures, marches, waltzes, clog dances and they had a chorus line of forty five girls.
That was in Los Angeles.

I was hired to play second trumpet and I was going to play under a famous circus man, he was well known all over the country for circuses and minstrel shows, and the first week his lip went out on him and so they moved me over to first chair, and they promoted him to get up and direct the band. First he was sitting down taking the cues from the piano player, so they gave him a stick with a light at the end of it so he could direct the band, because he was not only a good musician, he was a good writer and arranger, and they needed him.

You know that refutes the conception that many people have about jazz musicians as not being qualified to read the music, that you were saying that you had to play for many, many kinds of acts. You certainly had to be qualified.
Some say they had tough shows at the Cotton Club, because I played there with Caroline Snowden, but nothing was tougher than the burlesque show because they were all white.
All of the entertainers were white?
Oh, yes, the whole show was white.
Did they have any mixed bands at the time?
No.
The bands were all black?
All black. That's about all until 1930.
